oneLine: A five-reel video slot with fifty lines, free spins with a multiplier trail, a hold-and-win link with four jackpots and a fair gamble -- every feature won at the reels, never bought -- drawn entirely in SVG and canvas, sounded entirely by synthesis, and returning a measured 96.56%.
status: Feature complete, measured, and play-tested. 125 fast tests, typecheck, lint at zero warnings, a twenty-million-spin simulation returning 96.556% inside its target band, and a browser pass at four viewports with no console errors -- both features driven through their natural triggers, the gamble played through win, loss and collect, and reduced motion watched in both polarities. The mix is measured rather than argued about. What is left is a short, known list: see whatIsLeft, which is ordered.

whatIsLeft.detail: The largest remaining gap, and the only one that would block a real release. AUTOPLAY_COUNTS still offers Infinity with no loss limit, no single-win limit and no session reminder; autoplay stop conditions are a hard requirement in every regulated market. The shape that fits this cabinet: a loss limit and a single-win limit chosen when autoplay starts, both stopping the run rather than warning about it, plus a periodic reality check on elapsed time and net position. The autoplay menu already exists as a popover and is the natural home. Note the RTP disclosure that used to sit with this item is done -- it is on the attract screen.

src/app has no error.tsx and no global-error.tsx, and there is no React boundary anywhere. A throw during a hold-and-win render is a white screen, and because feature state is deliberately never persisted the player loses an in-flight link with no way back to it. The boundary needs to do more than apologise: it should offer to end the feature and settle at what is on the board, because the alternative is a player who watched nine orbs lock and got nothing. Small job, removes the worst failure mode in the app.

whatIsLeft.status: needs a person, not a tool
whatIsLeft.detail: It is now genuinely measured -- every cue rendered five times through a real Web Audio implementation, both loudness ladders monotonic, the limiter's behaviour on the pile-ups understood, and one real ordering bug found and fixed by measurement alone. But measurement is not listening, and what it cannot tell you is exactly what matters next: whether the GRAND is harsh where it is clamped, whether the reel loop grates across a long session, whether the fanfares wear out by the fifth time. Ten minutes on headphones.

whatIsLeft.item: Profile the FX layer on a real phone.
whatIsLeft.detail: A large canvas particle system that has only ever run on desktop. Reduced motion cuts it to 20% of particles so the accessible path is likely fine; the default path on a mid-range Android during a twenty-orb link is unmeasured.
The app installs as a PWA but still needs the network to load. Everything it serves is static and versioned, so this is a precache manifest rather than a caching strategy.

The four jackpots are fixed multiples of the stake. A jackpot that genuinely grows across sessions and players needs a server, and inventing one client-side would be a lie told in the most sensitive place on the machine. Listed so nobody mistakes it for an oversight.

architecture.engineIsPure: src/lib/engine is seeded, synchronous and side-effect free. spin(ctx) takes a generator, a stake and a mode and returns everything that spin did. It is the only thing that decides money.
architecture.storeNeverInventsMoney: src/lib/store debits, asks the engine, and pays exactly what came back. It deliberately does not import evaluateGrid at all -- a second opinion about what a board is worth is the bug you never find.
architecture.presentationIsPure: Every screen selects from useSlots and knows nothing else. The feature components take explicit props and are wired by FeatureOverlay, which is why they could be built before the store existed.
architecture.oneSeedOneSession: Every random word is drawn in an order documented at the top of spin.ts. That is what makes the RTP figure a measurement rather than an estimate, and what lets a disputed spin be replayed exactly.
architecture.moneyIsIntegerCents: Everywhere, with no exceptions. Line pays multiply betPerLine; scatter, orb and jackpot pays multiply totalBet. Confusing those two is the easiest way to be off by fifty times, so every field carrying a multiplier says which one it is.

keyDecisions.decision: The machine opens on an attract screen, and PLAY is the first thing a player presses.
keyDecisions.why: Partly because that is what a cabinet does, and partly for two concrete reasons. Browsers will not open an AudioContext without a gesture, and until this existed the first gesture might have been the spin button itself -- which made the machine's own opening cue the sound most likely to be swallowed. And it is where the measured return is stated: 96.56%, with the hit frequency, the volatility and the largest spin the committed simulation ever saw. A game that has measured itself to five decimal places and then declines to tell the player is being coy about the only number they are owed. `started` lives in the UI store and is deliberately not persisted: attract mode is where a cabinet sits when nobody is playing it.

keyDecisions.decision: There is no feature buy. Every feature is won at the reels.
keyDecisions.why: A buy button is an online-casino affordance, not a cabinet one, and it quietly changes what the machine is: the interesting question stops being 'will it come?' and becomes 'is it priced correctly?'. Dragon's Shrine is trying to be a machine you sit down at, so the shrine lights when the pearls land and not before. The engine's buy path (buyCost, buyForce, BUY_COSTS, the store's buyFeature) is deliberately kept and still asserted by the simulation, because forcing a trigger is how features get driven in a test or a browser now that no button does it -- but nothing in the cabinet can reach it.

keyDecisions.decision: No three.js and no Rapier, unlike the craps table next door.
keyDecisions.why: Craps needs a physics engine because its dice are rigid bodies whose landing must match what the RNG called. A slot cabinet is a 2D machine. SVG symbols with a canvas particle layer are crisper at every size, animate more cheaply, and ship 0.3 MB gzipped against craps' 1.4 MB.

keyDecisions.decision: Reel strips are declared as symbol counts per reel and expanded deterministically, rather than written out as bands.
keyDecisions.why: Tuning the return means moving one symbol's frequency on one reel, which is a single number in a count table and a needle in a haystack in a sixty-entry literal. The expansion spreads each symbol as evenly as its count allows, so a band cannot accidentally print four dragons in a row -- which reads as a broken reel whatever it does to the maths.

keyDecisions.decision: The wild never appears on reel 1 of the base band, and the dragon never takes reel 1 in free spins.
keyDecisions.why: A wild on the leftmost reel promotes every three of a kind to a four. It is a large and completely invisible chunk of return. In free spins the same asymmetry is worse: with reel 1 wild, a three-dragon-reel spin is fifty lines of five wilds and one spin outweighs the rest of the session.

keyDecisions.decision: MAJOR and GRAND are board awards -- won by filling eighteen or twenty cells -- and can never be carried by an orb.
keyDecisions.why: A top prize that can arrive unannounced on the first respin is a lottery ticket. One you can watch yourself approach is a feature.

keyDecisions.decision: The engine's draw order is pinned by a test that counts random words, not by one that checks a board.
keyDecisions.why: Retuning the strips changes every board and is a routine thing to do. Inserting or removing a draw silently invalidates every seeded expectation in the repository at once. The word-count assertion catches the second without being falsified by the first.

keyDecisions.decision: The store's test suite replays the engine to discover its own anchors rather than hard-coding seed and spin numbers.
keyDecisions.why: Its first draft did hard-code them, and they went stale within the hour when the maths lane retuned a draw. It now asks 'which spin of this seed triggers?' and asserts the store agrees, so it survives further tuning.

keyDecisions.decision: Persisted state is bankroll, stake, preferences, stats and history -- never a phase, a result, a feature or a spin token.
keyDecisions.why: A refresh in the middle of a hold-and-win would otherwise resume into a machine that cannot be finished. Asserted by the persistence tests.

keyDecisions.decision: Turbo scales every timing except the anticipation beats.
keyDecisions.why: A tease that is over before it registers is worse than no tease at all.

measured.note: The committed default. SIM_SPINS overrides the sample size for quick tuning runs, but the suite fails any run whose interval is wider than half the target band, so a short run cannot be mistaken for a measurement. Re-run 2026-08-31: 96.556% +/-0.595% over 20,000,000 spins, 8/8 green. An earlier draft of this file quoted 96.359% in its status line, which was simply wrong -- the `rtp` field here was right, and it is the figure the attract screen now shows the player.

buys.note: The buy buttons are gone from the cabinet -- see keyDecisions. The prices and their assertions are kept because the simulation still proves the forced-trigger path returns less than the base game, which is what makes the engine's `force` safe to use for testing.

trapsWorthKnowing: Money is integer cents everywhere, and line pays multiply betPerLine while scatter, orb and jackpot pays multiply totalBet. Confusing the two is a factor-of-fifty error that still typechecks. Every field carrying a multiplier says which one it is; keep it that way.

The store never asks what a board is worth. It debits, calls the engine, and pays exactly what came back -- it does not import evaluateGrid at all. A second opinion about a board's value is the bug you never find. The store tests assert `bankroll === STARTING_BANKROLL - wagered + won` after every settled spin, which catches that whole class in one line.

There are two layouts. The `tight` variant (short and wide -- a landscape phone) puts the deck in a ~265px rail beside the board while the viewport is 812px wide, so `sm:` utilities are actively wrong inside that rail. The variant is declared after the Tailwind import so its utilities sort last and win. Any deck or meter change has to be checked in both.

Never measure a loop or a music bed inside an offline audio render. Their schedulers are setInterval, which keeps wall time and knows nothing about render time, and one of them will cheerfully report the limiter's ceiling for an ordinary spin that actually peaks at 0.358. Measure them alone. See tools/measure-audio.md.

One audio render is not a measurement. The noise buffer is regenerated per context and noiseTrim can multiply a narrowband voice by twelve, so a single render of dragonReel lands anywhere between 0.32 and 0.79. Take the median of five.

ifYouChangeOneThing.theStrips: Re-run npm run test:stats. The strips are the whole feel of the machine and every number in paytable.ts is tuned against them. Then re-measure the buy prices -- do not scale them by eye.
ifYouChangeOneThing.theDrawOrder: Expect engine.test.ts's draw-order pin to fail, and know that every seeded expectation in both suites has moved at the same time.
ifYouChangeOneThing.theContracts: src/lib/engine/types.ts and src/lib/store/contract.ts are published: add to them, never rename or remove. Everything else compiles against them.
ifYouChangeOneThing.theLayout: There are two layouts, not one. `tight` in globals.css (short and wide) puts the deck in a rail beside the board; everything else stacks. The rail is ~265px wide while the viewport is 812px, so `sm:` utilities are actively wrong inside it -- that is why the tight variant is declared after the Tailwind import, so its utilities sort last and win. Check both.
ifYouChangeOneThing.aFanfare: Re-run the harness in tools/measure-audio.md and check the one invariant at the bottom of it: jackpotGrand must be louder than winLegendary. It was not, for the whole of the previous handoff, and nothing but a measurement would have caught it.

verifiedBy.fastTests: 125 passing in about two seconds (71 engine, 54 store)
verifiedBy.simulation: 8/8 passing over 20,000,000 seeded spins, re-run 2026-08-31 at 96.556% +/-0.595%.
verifiedBy.build: production static export, 0.9 MB of JS, 0.3 MB gzipped
verifiedBy.browser: Chromium at 1440x900, 768x1024 (tablet), 375x812 (portrait phone) and 812x375 (landscape phone). Zero console errors throughout, and no page scroll in either axis at any of the four. Base game: loads, spins, paytable correct. Free spins: triggered NATURALLY from a probed seed (not bought) -- ten spins, counter counts down, multiplier trail steps, feature total accumulates to $14.60 and the bankroll agrees. Hold and win: triggered naturally -- nine orbs lock, respins reset, board settles at $21.00 and the bankroll agrees. Gamble: offered on a 4x win, played a losing call, a winning call (black doubled $4 to $8) and a collect, bankroll correct after each. Takeover: a 50.4x MEGA counted up to $50.40 and matched the engine to the cent. Reduced motion: watched in both polarities -- the takeover still says everything it said, faster and calmer.
verifiedBy.audio: Every cue rendered through Chromium's OfflineAudioContext at 44.1 kHz, five renders each, median reported; peak and the RMS of the loudest 300 ms window. Both ladders climb and neither crosses the other, the GRAND leads a LEGENDARY by 0.62 dB, nothing is inaudible (quietest is meterCount at -40.7) and the pile-ups behave: an ordinary spin peaks at 0.358 and only the jackpot cases reach the limiter. The harness and its three traps are in tools/measure-audio.md -- the sharpest being that loops must never be measured inside an offline render, because their setInterval schedulers keep wall time and will report the limiter's ceiling for an ordinary spin.
